To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
auditory interneurons in metathoracic, abdominal and suboesophageal ganglia of the locust are involved in the control of flight steering, and that these interneurons are sensitive to sound.
the auditory interneurons in metathoracic (T3) ganglion can activate the locust flight system (Fig. 5) or can drive directional head and abdomen movement (Figs.6,7,9,12).

auditory interneurons can drive flight steering behavior in tethered animals and that these interneurons can be classified into three functional classes: (1) flight oscillator neurons, (2) neurons that activate the abdomen and the head to the same side, (3) neurons that activate one of the two antagonistic steering systems (the abdomen and the head) in opposite directions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of auditory interneurons and their output function in the locust nervous system.
the question of whether auditory interneurons are capable of driving the flight steering system of locusts.

the analysis of the neuronal substrate for the processing of acoustic information in the locust, and with the identification of the neuronal mechanisms underlying flight steering and the phonotactic behavior of the animals.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the auditory interneurons of the locust are involved in the steering behavior of the animal, which can be elicited by ultrasound pulses of frequencies between 10 and 15 kHz.
auditory interneurons in metathoracic locusts are involved in flight steering and that they can be subdivided into three functional groups.
the auditory interneurons of the metathorax are involved in the generation of steering movements of the head, the abdomen and of flight.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the auditory interneurons in metathoracic locusts are able to drive the steering behavior of the locusts in the same direction as in intact animals, but they cannot produce the steering behavior in the opposite direction.

auditory interneurons in metathoracic locusts can drive the steering behavior of the animal in 2 ways: (1) they can activate the flight oscillator and (2) they can drive head and abdomen movements, which are the components of steering.

auditory interneurons can drive the flight oscillator, can produce directional movements of the head, and can drive the head and abdomen in opposite directions, which are components of bat avoidance behavior.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the same auditory interneurons that are activated by ultrasound pulses in intact tethered animals are also activated when the same animals are stimulated with pure tones.
we have shown that a single neuron, an auditory interneuron, can control both head and abdomen movements in a locust.
the same interneurons that drive the flight system also drive the steering behavior.
